Promise-Aware ETA and Delivery-Promise Optimization

Author: Your Name  |  Program: M.S. (CS/Data Science)  |  Date: 01 Nov 2025

Abstract

Accurate delivery-time prediction is necessary but insufficient for high-quality customer promises in e-commerce. The decisive element is the promise policy—the mapping from predictive uncertainty to a quoted delivery window that balances late deliveries against unnecessarily long promises. Using the public Olist corpus and a reproducible synthetic bench, we learn calibrated quantile predictors for delivery lead time and optimize policies under asymmetric costs. An offline simulator links model quality to operational outcomes, and fairness diagnostics quantify regional and seller-level disparities. Calibrated high-quantile policies (τ≈0.90) reduce expected cost relative to point-estimate baselines while maintaining interpretable guarantees.

1. Introduction

Customer promises drive conversion, satisfaction, and last-mile cost. Traditional ETA systems focus on point forecasts and add fixed buffers, which fail under heavy-tailed, heteroscedastic delays caused by geography, seller dispatch practices, and exogenous shocks. This thesis reframes promise setting as decision-making under predictive uncertainty: we model the conditional distribution of lead time and select a quantile policy pτ(x)=Qτ(Y|X=x) to control late risk and promise length explicitly.

Thesis statement. Uncertainty-aware prediction paired with cost-aware policy optimization yields auditable, efficient delivery promises using only purchase-time signals.

Contributions. (i) Leakage-safe feature learning at purchase time; (ii) calibrated quantile modeling (split-conformal, CQR); (iii) an offline simulator that maps distributions to Late-Promise Rate (LPR), Average Promise Days (APD), and composite cost; (iv) fairness diagnostics over geography and sellers; (v) a public, reproducible pipeline and artifact suite suitable for academic evaluation.

2. Related Work

Delivery-time prediction. Early approaches use survival analysis and queueing-theoretic models with strong parametric assumptions; recent work adopts tree ensembles and deep sequence models over courier events. Our focus is purchase-time promises, avoiding downstream event leakage while supporting interpretable policies.

Quantile regression. Linear quantile regression (Koenker & Bassett) and tree-based quantile estimators (e.g., LightGBM quantile) enable direct conditional quantile estimation without distributional assumptions, which is critical in heavy-tailed logistics.

Conformal prediction. Split-conformal prediction and Conformalized Quantile Regression (CQR) furnish finite-sample coverage under exchangeability, yielding calibrated intervals that translate directly into promise bands. We leverage these to guarantee reliability targets.

Decision-focused evaluation. There is increasing emphasis on evaluating ML in terms of downstream policies and utility. We operationalize this by optimizing τ against business-weighted costs and auditing fairness trade-offs.

3. Data

3.1 Olist public dataset

We use orders, customers, sellers, items, payments, geolocation, and reviews. Key timestamps are standardized to UTC and validated for monotonicity (e.g. approval ≤ carrier pickup ≤ delivery). We remove obviously corrupted rows and document assumptions (e.g., imputations for missing freight).

3.2 Target and labels

The target Y is lead time (days) from order approval to delivery. Labels are computed with strict timestamp order; outliers are capped for robustness in model selection but kept for policy evaluation.

3.3 Train/validation/test splits

Temporal splits emulate deployment: training on early periods and validation/testing on later periods. This stresses generalization under drift and prevents leakage from future orders.

3.4 Data governance

We include a provenance log, schema checks, and a data dictionary; scripts materialize immutable snapshots under data/raw and data/processed.

4. Methodology

4.1 Feature Engineering (purchase-time only)

  • Basket & payment: item count, total value, freight; payment type and installments.
  • Geography: haversine distance via zipcode-prefix medians for customer/seller coordinates.
  • Seller dispatch: trailing median and P90 dispatch lag; trailing order volumes; ship-before-limit share; recent-versus-baseline drift. Computed with rolling windows (30/60/90d) anchored strictly before the focal order.
  • Product mix: total weight/volume and category diversity indicators.
  • Seasonality: month, day-of-week, hour, and optional holiday flags.
Leakage guards. For order i at time ti, aggregates only consider events with timestamp < ti. Sparse histories back off to global medians and expose a coverage mask.

4.2 Models

We fit Linear Quantile Regression, Histogram-based Gradient Boosting (quantile), and LightGBM (quantile) across τ ∈ {0.50,0.80,0.90,0.95}. Hyperparameters are tuned with temporal CV, optimizing mean pinball loss.

4.3 Calibration

We adopt split-conformal wrappers and CQR to deliver target coverage (e.g., 90%). Diagnostics report empirical coverage, lower/upper violation rates, and interval width. Calibration is performed on a held-out calibration fold and refreshed in rolling-origin analyses.

4.4 Promise Policy

Promises quote the upper quantile pτ(x). We evaluate LPR = E[1\{Y > pτ(X)\}], APD = E[pτ(X)], and composite cost C(τ)=λlateLPR + λslowAPD. Segment-aware variants compute the same metrics by distance decile, category, and seller-dispatch decile.

4.5 Offline Simulator

The simulator ingests predictions and intervals, sweeps τ, and computes LPR/APD/C with bootstrap confidence intervals. It exports global and segment tables used for selection and fairness audits.

4.6 Fairness Analysis

We report coverage, average lateness/earliness, expected cost, and support per group (region, seller). Disparities are summarized as differences and ratios relative to a reference group. We also experiment with constrained policies that cap disparity at selection time.

4.7 Implementation

Code is modularized under src/promise_aware_eta with pipelines, modeling, and policy modules; experiments/ houses runners and logs; configs/ contains canonical YAMLs. MLflow tracks metrics and artifacts.

5. Experiments

Protocol. (1) Materialize features; (2) train baseline quantile models; (3) calibrate; (4) simulate policies; (5) evaluate fairness; (6) ablate features and test robustness (rolling-origin, outlier handling). We report pinball loss, coverage error, interval width, LPR, APD, composite cost, and fairness gaps with confidence intervals where appropriate.

6. Results

6.1 Calibration

After split-conformalization, observed coverage approaches but does not fully match the 90% target on the final test slice; violation decomposition indicates slightly more upper misses, suggesting modest right-tail underestimation and motivating τ adjustment and/or residual recalibration.

6.2 Policy Selection

Global minimum expected cost is achieved at τ=0.90, with a substantial LPR reduction at moderate APD increase relative to τ=0.50. Sensitivity analysis over λlate:λslow demonstrates robust optimality of high quantiles within practical ranges (e.g., 10:1 to 30:1).

6.3 Fairness

Regional coverage spans 0.84–0.93 with north as reference; seller-level coverage ranges 0.79–1.00. Disparities concentrate among sparse-history sellers; monitoring sample sizes and applying shrinkage are essential to avoid overreacting to noise.

6.4 Robustness

Rolling-origin calibration shows slow drift; a monthly recalibration cadence maintains coverage within ±0.02. Feature ablations confirm seller-dispatch and geography as key drivers; removing either inflates right-tail error and interval width.

7. Discussion

Promises should be managed as policies with explicit levers (τ and λ). Calibrated quantiles provide a principled interface for SRE-style monitoring (coverage, violation mix, width) and business trade-offs (LPR vs APD). Segment-aware policies add complexity; our data suggest a globally optimal τ with segment-level cost variability, making a phased deployment reasonable.

8. Limitations & Ethics

Olist lacks courier telemetry and chain-of-custody events, limiting causal analysis and intervention modeling. Offline simulation cannot capture behavioral feedback (e.g., sellers accelerating dispatch if promises tighten). Fairness estimates in small segments are volatile; reports should include support, and constrained optimization should cap disparities.

9. Reproducibility

We provide frozen environments, feature snapshot hashes, and canonical YAML configs. MLflow/W&B track metrics and artifacts. Release artifacts include predictions, calibrated intervals, policy tables, and fairness exports for independent replication.

CLI. python experiments/run_stage_pipeline.py --config configs/experiments/quantile_baseline_lightgbm.yaml --outdir experiments/logs/ --seed 42

10. Conclusion

Promise-aware ETA reframes delivery promises as optimization over calibrated predictive quantiles. With only purchase-time signals and public data, the method yields interpretable guarantees, cost-efficient policies, and actionable fairness diagnostics, and it integrates cleanly with MLOps instrumentation.
